claim: The once-flag is ONE shared surface across the two runtimes, not two private ones (P1: the tick wakes replan_pending ONCE; AGENTS rule 2: one behavior). On a reached, un-closed horizon, after tick.sh wakes replan_pending for phase X, the very next tick.py tick on the same project sleeps replan_waiting (no second wake), and after a tick.py wake the next tick.sh tick sleeps likewise; the file .hb/.replan-alerted holds exactly the phase-id bytes with no trailing newline whichever runtime wrote it (od -c identical). tests/horizon.sh must run at least one mixed-runtime wake-then-tick sequence (a tick.sh wake followed by a tick.py tick, or the reverse) asserting replan_waiting, so that the idiomatic wrong implementation — tick.sh writing the flag with `echo "$RP_PHASE" > "$REPLAN_FLAG"` (a trailing newline that tick.py's raw read never matches) — goes red. Pre-probed as a real behaviour bug: with that mutant, tick.py wakes replan_pending a SECOND time for H2 straight after the tick.sh wake (the real tree sleeps), yet tests/horizon.sh prints HORIZON-OK; parity has no horizon tick case and pytest has no replan test at all.
violation: A tick by the other runtime, run directly after a replan_pending wake with no cure between, wakes replan_pending again for the same phase instead of sleeping replan_waiting; or od -c of .hb/.replan-alerted differs by which tick wrote it; or a copy of the repo with tick.sh's flag write changed to echo (trailing newline) still prints HORIZON-OK from tests/horizon.sh.

claim: Neither tick appends ANY event on the replan wake or on the replan_waiting sleeps — the log records decisions, not notifications (h1b; P1's once-only wake has no log footprint) — and the proof pins this for tick.py, not only tick.sh. On a reached, un-closed horizon, a wake followed by two waiting ticks on EACH runtime leaves events.jsonl byte-identical to its pre-tick bytes (f3 pins this for tick.sh via HB_NOTIFY_CMD; nothing pins tick.py). tests/horizon.sh must count events around the tick.py wake and waiting ticks, so that a tick.py whose _replan_wake logs a 'wake' event (the per-task wake-logging pattern its own task branch uses) goes red. Pre-probed as a test gap: that mutant appends {"event":"wake","reason":"replan_pending","phase":"H2"} on the python wake (7 -> 8 lines) and tests/horizon.sh still prints HORIZON-OK; pytest has no replan test.
violation: events.jsonl gains any line across a replan_pending wake or a replan_waiting sleep on either runtime; or a copy of the repo whose tick.py appends an event in the replan wake path still prints HORIZON-OK from tests/horizon.sh.

claim: The drivers' NAMED escalation names the horizon (P3: a NAMED escalation, HB-EXEC STOP: replan_pending; h1b: the named case is honesty). On every run at an open horizon — the run that sees the wake and each later replan_waiting run — both hb-exec.js run and hb exec run print 'HB-EXEC STOP: replan_pending — <phase id>' with the phase id present (H2 on the fixture; after appending a flagged H3 and completing it through the CLI, H3), identically on both drivers and whichever runtime's tick consumed the wake. tests/horizon.sh m4 must assert the phase id on the stop line, not only the prefix, so that deleting executor.py's named replan_pending case — whose default branch prints the bare 'HB-EXEC STOP: replan_pending' and so still satisfies every current grep — goes red, as would a tick that drops data.phase from the wake or the replan_waiting sleep. Pre-probed as a test gap: with the python named case removed, the wake run prints 'HB-EXEC STOP: replan_pending' with no phase while the waiting runs and the node driver print '— H2', and tests/horizon.sh still prints HORIZON-OK.
violation: Any HB-EXEC STOP line at an open horizon, on either driver, on the wake run or a later waiting run, lacks the horizon phase id (or names the wrong phase after an appended horizon is reached); or the executor.py named-case-removed mutant leaves tests/horizon.sh green.
